transcript.content: Hello, it's nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

Nice to meet you, too. Well, I guess what brought me in is... I just can't stop jumping out of my skin lately. I do maintenance work, and if a breaker snaps, or someone drops a tool, or even if somebody just comes up behind me when I'm not looking, I practically jump out of my boots. 

And the thing is, it doesn't just stop there. My heart just keeps hammering in my chest long after everyone else has moved on and gone back to work. It's just getting to be too much to deal with.
Have you experienced or witnessed a traumatic event that these reactions began after?
Yeah... yeah, I did. This whole thing has been going on since an arc-flash accident on a retrofit job I was working on. It's been, well, about a year and a month now since that happened.
Since the arc-flash accident, have you had unwanted memories, nightmares, or flashbacks about what happened?

Yeah, I do. It's... well, it just comes out of nowhere. I could just be standing there loading tools into the truck, and suddenly I'll see that bright flash right in my head, or I'll hear the trainee yelling. It just knocks me sideways. It feels exactly like it's happening all over again right then and there.
Since the accident, have you been avoiding people, places, activities, or conversations that remind you of what happened?

Yeah, I do. I actually... I make excuses not to go near certain panels or breakers anymore. Same with certain job sites, I just try to get out of going to them. And I definitely don't talk about that day with anyone. I avoid it completely. Because... well, once that stuff starts playing in my head, I just can't shut it off.
Since the accident, have you felt emotionally numb or detached from other people?

Yeah, I'd say so. It's like... even when my wife or the kids try to joke around with me, or if something good actually happens at work, I just don't feel it. It's like there's this wall inside me. I can't feel happy or... or anything good, really, even when I know I should.

The duration and symptom pattern support post-traumatic stress disorder rather than acute stress disorder or panic disorder.
